text:
A: Hello.
B: Hello. I'm Prajakta.
A: Karen. Sorry, Pra—
B: Prajakta.
A: Prajakta. Got it.
B: Your kitchen is very tidy. I noticed it on the photo earlier.
A: Thank you. It has to be, or I can't think. Yours isn't bad either.
B: It's not usually like this. I tidied before the call. When I'm stressed I reorganise the cupboards.
A: That's not a bad habit to have.
B: My husband thinks it is. He can't find anything afterwards.
A: That's his problem.
B: Yes, that's what I tell him.
A: So what do you do?
B: Quality control in a pharmaceutical lab. In Stevenage. I test batches before they're released.
A: Right. So if you get it wrong, someone gets the wrong tablets.
B: Basically. That's why I check everything twice. Some people in my lab don't. They write things in the notebook half done and then I have to chase them.
A: Oh, I know that one. I do admin for a haulage firm. Drivers' timesheets, vehicle schedules, purchase orders. If one form's wrong, a lorry's off the road, or we fail a compliance check, and guess whose desk that lands on. Not the bloke who couldn't be bothered to fill in a box.
B: Yes. And nobody remembers that you fixed it.
A: No. They just remember if it went wrong.
B: I had a team leader before who did that. Blamed me for someone else's mistake in front of everyone. I still think about it.
A: Did you say anything?
B: I did. It didn't help. He moved on, but nobody ever said sorry.
A: They never do. My lot take it for granted. I've been there eleven years and my title's still "administrator". I basically run the place.
B: You should ask for it in writing.
A: I have. Twice.
B: Then ask a third time. With a list of what you actually do.
A: That's not a bad idea, actually. I've got it all on a spreadsheet anyway.
B: Of course you have.
A: Of course I have. Is that your little one's bag on the chair?
B: Yes, Ira. She's seven. The school sends emails at nine o'clock at night saying tomorrow is non-uniform day, bring a pound. Every time.
A: Nothing changes. Mine's seventeen and I had that for ten years. It doesn't get easier, you just stop caring about the pound.
B: I don't think I will stop caring. I worry about everything with her.
A: You do. Even at seventeen. He's on an electrical apprenticeship, and I still worry he'll electrocute himself.
B: That's a reasonable worry.
A: I thought so. Nobody else does.
B: Do you have help? Family nearby?
A: My mum, she's in Crawley. She's seventy-eight now, so it's more me helping her these days. Yours?
B: In Pune. India. My mother-in-law comes for a few months, but my parents are there. It's far.
A: That must be hard.
B: It is. I don't really—
